newsitem.title: UK: Northern Ireland's economy gets double jobs boost.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland's economy gets double jobs boost.

text.p: Northern Ireland announced another fall in unemployment and a 78 million pound ($123 million) job-creating expansion on Wednesday, weeks after IRA guerrillas halted their war against British rule.
The government said seasonally-adjusted unemployment fell in July by 2,100 to 60,500, or 7.9 percent of the workforce, from 11.3 percent in July 1996.
Unadjusted unemployment rose in real terms by 4,336 to 65,135 but dropped proportionally to 8.5 percent of the labour force from 11.8 a year ago, the department of economic development said.

The figures, which confirmed a downward trend stretching back for more than a year, were released on the day that a U.S. multinational announced a major expansion in the province's second city, Londonderry.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said DuPont was setting up a new state-of-the-art automated plant to meet European demand for the elastane fibre Lycra.

She told reporters the project, to be backed by the government's Industrial Development Board, was an example of the economic fruits the province could enjoy afer the Irish Republican Army (IRA) called a truce on July 20.
"DuPont's endorsement is the most significant development since the IRA ceasefire," she said.
The 78 million pound expansion will also secure 450 jobs at DuPont's Maydown site, the largest Lycra fibre production operation in Europe.
Mowlam said in a statement that the expansion showed Northern Ireland was "a good place to do business".

"It is particularly important because it is one of the strongest signals ever by a leader of corporate America to the international business community, especially in the United States, of the strength of Northern Ireland's business case."
DuPont (UK) managing director Bill Walker said: "This expansion represents our continued confidence in both the European market and our operations in Northern Ireland."
DuPont, which chose Northern Ireland in 1960, employs almost 1,000 people in Londonderry and is one of the biggest exporters in the province.
The scheme was announced weeks after the IRA called a new truce in its 28-year war against British rule in a bid to get its political wing, Sinn Fein, to peace talks in September.
Britain says Northern Ireland's economy has proved robust and has in many sectors shrugged off the effects of three decades of a political and sectarian conflict that has killed 3,200 people.
It says the Northern Ireland economy, once a regional black spot, is now performing as well as many other British regions and better than most.
But business leaders say it could attract further foreign investment if pro-British and pro-Irish political groups join the September peace talks.

Sinn Fein says it will be there when the talks open on September 15 but the province's key Protestant group, the Ulster Unionist Party, has not made clear whether it will negotiate with Sinn Fein or not.
It says the July 20 ceasefire is a ruse and that the IRA will return to war if it does not get the kind of settlement it seeks. ($ = 0.633 British Pounds)
